Nestling development in the Slender-billed prion (Pachyptila belcheri) has been documented primarily from colonies on the Kerguelen Archipelago, where climatic conditions impose a tight seasonal breeding schedule. Field studies indicate that newly hatched chicks weigh approximately 25 grams [Wwb = approximately 25 grams], a relatively modest mass given the semi-precocial developmental mode typical of procellariiform seabirds. This initial investment allows the altricial nestling to rely on yolk reserves during the first few days before regular parental provisioning becomes established. The incubation period culminates after roughly 30.5 days [ab = roughly 30.5 days] when eggs are maintained at an average temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that balances embryonic metabolic demand with the constraints of intermittent incubation shifts. Upon hatching, the nestling chick enters a phase of rapid mass gain, sustained by the frequent delivery of lipid-rich stomach oil and partially digested prey items by both parents. This early period is characterized by steady feather growth and progressive thermoregulatory capacity, which are crucial for survival in the cool, windswept burrows that serve as nurseries. The relatively low hatchling mass compared to the ultimate adult size underscores the extent of the post-hatching growth trajectory that must be completed before independence.

During the extended nestling phase, the developing chick undergoes a remarkable transformation, culminating in an asymptotic body mass of 250 grams [Wwi = 250 grams]. This ultimate wet weight represents the plateau reached by the nestling as it approaches fledging, a value that is comparable to the adult mass and reflects the substantial accumulation of fat reserves required for a sustained post-fledging period at sea. Growth curve analyses from marked individuals show that this plateau is achieved after a period of rapid linear gain, followed by a gradual deceleration as the nestling redirects resources toward feather maturation and behavioral preparation for departure. Consistent with observations in other Pachyptila species, the mass gain is not perfectly monotonic; periodic fluctuations occur in response to variation in parental provisioning success, which can be driven by local prey availability and weather conditions. The comparison between the initial weight of 25 grams [Wwb = 25 grams] and the final asymptote of 250 grams [Wwi = 250 grams] illustrates a tenfold increase, a ratio that is typical for procellariiform seabirds and indicative of the high metabolic efficiency of these nestlings during the rapid growth phase. The accumulation of this mass is a critical prerequisite for the subsequent milestone of fledging.

The timing of the major post-hatching events in Pachyptila belcheri follows a predictable schedule under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, which involve a body temperature of approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. Under these conditions, the fledging stage is typically reached at 50 days after hatching [tx = 50 days after hatching], marking the point at which the chick achieves sustained flight and departs the natal burrow at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This relatively short nestling period, compared to larger procellariids, is a consequence of the species' small body size and the selective pressure to fledge before the onset of severe winter weather in their subantarctic breeding grounds. The fledgling, once it leaves the burrow, must rapidly become nutritionally independent, though some post-fledging parental care has been documented near the colony. Achieving flight at this developmental stage requires the completion of feather maturation and the attainment of sufficient wing loading, both of which are supported by the accumulated body reserves from the nestling phase. The age at fledging represents a crucial life-history transition, after which the immature bird faces its first extended foraging trip over the Southern Ocean, a period of high mortality risk for naive individuals.

Gonadal development and the attainment of reproductive competence follow a considerably longer trajectory than the nestling phase. The onset of puberty in Slender-billed prions occurs at approximately 150 days after hatching [tp = approximately 150 days after hatching] when maintained at an internal body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This milestone, which involves the activation of gametogenesis and the onset of gonadal swelling, is not immediately followed by breeding activity. Instead, young birds typically defer their first reproductive attempt for several years, aligning with the broader life-history pattern of delayed maturity common among long-lived seabirds. The initial maturation of the reproductive system at this age is a prerequisite for later breeding, but successful reproduction also requires the acquisition of foraging skills and the establishment of a nest site within the colony, both of which take additional time. The gap between gonadal maturity and first breeding is thought to reflect the time needed for young birds to accumulate sufficient body condition and social experience to compete for burrows and mates. The high energy demands of reproduction in this unpredictable environment thus select for a cautious onset of breeding activity.

The culmination of the pre-breeding period is marked by the first brood, which in this species occurs at 2 years since birth [tR = 2 years since birth] under a body temperature regime of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This initial reproductive event is a critical life-history milestone, and successful pairs typically produce a single egg per breeding attempt. Clutch size is invariably one egg per nest [N_R_i = one egg per nest], and annual breeding frequency is limited to a single nesting attempt per year [F_R_i = single nesting attempt per year], a reflection of the high energetic cost of producing and incubating a large, yolk-rich egg in the cold subantarctic environment. This combination of a single-egg clutch and an annual breeding cycle represents a very low maximum reproductive rate, which is compensated for by an exceptionally long lifespan. The oldest documented individuals of Pachyptila belcheri have been recorded surviving for as long as 25 years [am = 25 years] under natural conditions at a core body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This extended longevity, combined with high annual adult survival, is typical of procellariiform seabirds and allows multiple breeding attempts across a lifetime, which is necessary to offset the low per-capita reproductive output. The demographic strategy thus relies on persistence and iteroparity rather than high fecundity.
